purpose: Azacitidine is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It helps slow down the growth of abnormal blood cells and encourages your bone marrow to make healthier blood cells. It is often used when other treatments have not worked or are not suitable.
how_it_works: Your DNA has chemical tags that can turn genes on or off. In cancer cells, some important genes that stop cancer growth get incorrectly switched off. Azacitidine works by removing those wrong chemical tags, helping to switch those protective genes back on. This slows down or stops the cancer cells from growing and spreading.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are very common. You may feel tired, have low appetite, or get constipation. Injection site reactions like redness, bruising, or soreness can happen if you get the shot form. Low blood counts are common, which can make you more prone to infections, bruising, or feeling weak and short of breath.
warnings: Because azacitidine lowers your blood cell counts, you are at higher risk for serious infections, bleeding, and anemia — tell your doctor right away if you have a fever, unusual bruising, or feel very short of breath. Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm a baby. Men and women should use reliable birth control during treatment and for a period after finishing. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as some can interact with this drug.
typical_dosing: The dose and schedule depend on which condition is being treated and whether you receive it as an injection under the skin, into a vein, or as a tablet. A common schedule for injections is once daily for 7 days in a row, repeated every 4 weeks (one cycle). The oral tablet form is usually taken once daily for 14 days every 28 days. Your cancer care team will determine the exact dose that is right for you.
